## How to use this map

The legacy source is `sandbox/madagascar_clinic_data_cleaning/scripts/`.
This page maps all 11 files in that directory to the pipeline notebooks that
carry, or would carry, their responsibilities. The summaries below come from
reading those files and the current notebooks; the legacy scripts were not
executed to prepare this map. Counts recorded in legacy comments are historical
observations, not newly verified results.

Source links use GitHub line anchors pinned to the local legacy checkout's
commit `31e0769683e133e136b09ac0c6608c5a12657a9a`. The line ranges and file contents were
checked locally against that commit; the GitHub URLs were not accessed. Pinning
the revision keeps these references stable if the upstream branch changes.
References to commented code are identified as such in the descriptions.

Artifact paths in the script summaries retain the legacy layout and spelling
so that missing or inconsistent handoffs remain visible. They describe the
old workflow; replacement storage locations still follow the new project's
staging and release contracts.

**Existing, in development** means a replacement notebook contains relevant
code, not that migration or equivalence testing is complete. **Proposed** means
the destination notebook does not yet exist. Proposed names describe a possible
continuation of the current notebook sequence; they do not create targets or
settle how many execution steps each notebook should contain.

Each implementation notebook should explain the scientific operation before
its code: what one row represents, which input supplies each decision, what
changes between stages, and what evidence would establish that the result is
correct. A notebook can contain several targets while retaining one coherent
responsibility.

## How the responsibilities connect

Three different kinds of mapping are involved. The **facility mapping** links
a year-specific GESIS code to a DHIS2 facility UID. The **clinic identity
crosswalk** follows a clinic through code and name changes. The **diagnosis
dictionary** defines comparable measurement variables across reporting systems.
The first two identify who reported; the third defines what was reported.

The spatial branch assigns administrative areas called fokontany (FKT) to
clinics and unions their polygons into healthsheds. These are based on the
2022 sectorization. Their use alongside earlier reporting data does not itself
establish historical catchment boundaries.

The diagram shows the intended scientific handoffs, including proposed
notebooks. It is a responsibility map, not a claim that all these dependencies
are already implemented in `_targets.R`.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  W3["18: Prepare Wave 3"] --> D["21 proposed: Diagnosis dictionary"]
  M["19: Clean facility mapping"] --> I["20: Construct clinic IDs"]
  M --> H["23 proposed: Sectorization and healthsheds"]
  W3 --> C["22 proposed: Clean diagnosis data"]
  D --> C
  I --> C
  I --> L["24 proposed: Locate clinics"]
  H --> L
  C -->|Reporting history| F["25 proposed: Combine clinic metadata"]
  I --> F
  H --> F
  L --> F
```

The Wave 3 preparation script also reads the original facility mapping to
attach descriptive columns. It does not read the cleaned mapping produced by
script 1. That separate use is described below because it affects join
cardinality and should remain visible during migration.

## 0 — Prepare the Wave 3 source table

**Source:** [0_prep_w3_kevin_translated.R][legacy-w3].
**Destination:** [18_page-prep-w3.qmd](../18_page-prep-w3.qmd).

This script translates the earlier Wave 3 preparation into R. It recursively
reads the RMA CSV exports, adjusts inferred logical columns to numeric so that
sparsely populated measurements can be read, drops two organisation-unit
description/code fields, and combines the tables. It then groups by
`organisationunitid` and `periodname`, taking the maximum of each remaining
field and replacing numeric negative infinity from all-missing groups with
missing values. This is a maximum rule, not an addition of reports.
See [CSV type handling, lines 25–38][w3-reader];
[file discovery, column removal, and combination, lines 43–81][w3-ingest];
[maximum reduction, lines 161–168][w3-max].

Next, it reads the original DHIS2–GESIS mapping, selects facility UID, GESIS
code, type, and name, removes exact duplicates and missing UIDs, and joins
those attributes to the Wave 3 data by UID alone. It adds the legacy `V1` row
index. Finally, for periods after `202300`, it substitutes three renamed
breastfeeding and mosquito-net fields into their earlier column names and
drops the replacement columns.
See [crosswalk preparation, lines 191–212][w3-crosswalk];
[UID join and row index, lines 233–243][w3-join];
[period-specific substitutions, lines 264–272][w3-substitutions].

**Handoff:** the script writes
`data/raw/from_Kevin/wave3_with_keys_may2_v3.csv`. Scripts 3 and 4A instead read
`wave3_with_keys.csv`. The prepared table supplies both measurements and the
column names/order used by the diagnosis dictionary.
See [script 0 output, lines 274–275][w3-output];
[script 3 input and column numbering, lines 31–48][dictionary-w3-input];
[script 4A input, line 249][diagnosis-w3-input].

**Context for notebook 18:** explain the two reductions now used to avoid
holding all source tables in R: maximum within each file, then maximum across
the file summaries. Explain all-missing behavior separately from zero values.
The UID-only descriptive join can repeat a row when a UID has several mapping
records; grouping the mapping by UID in the legacy script did not make it
unique. Record the expected cardinality rather than assuming one UID implies
one output row. The script's opening comment limits scope to 2020–2022, but its
reader is recursive and its final substitutions explicitly address 2023; the
actual supported input period needs an explicit contract.
See [stated scope, lines 1–6][w3-scope];
[recursive reader, lines 51–53][w3-recursion];
[2023 substitutions, lines 264–272][w3-substitutions].

The replacement notebook already contains the per-file DuckDB reader and
reducer, cross-file reduction, descriptive join, and substitutions. Its
stopping-point prose and crosswalk input variable names are not yet consistent
with all of that code. Treat it as a migration in progress.

## 1 — Clean the DHIS2–GESIS facility mapping

**Source:** [1_clean_mapping_dhis2_gesis.R][legacy-mapping].
**Destination:** [19_page-clean-mapping-dhis2-gesis.qmd](../19_page-clean-mapping-dhis2-gesis.qmd).

This script prepares the bridge between historical GESIS facility codes and
DHIS2 UIDs. It reads the original mapping and gives the four UID columns
explicit region, district, commune, and facility names. It removes 2022 and
the invalid `Belalanda` code, applies reviewed GESIS-code corrections, and
fills a known missing facility UID.
See [source mapping and exclusions, lines 11–18][mapping-input];
[code checks, corrections, and known UID fill, lines 25–58][mapping-corrections].

The remaining work applies the reviewed workbooks and CSVs: fill other missing
UIDs; interpret annotations for UID-years associated with multiple GESIS
codes as keep, rename, or delete decisions; add reviewed codes absent from the
original mapping; and apply individual corrections discovered while comparing
the mapping with diagnosis data. Deletions use the relevant year, code, and
UID so that an unrelated record sharing a code is not removed accidentally.
See [additional UID fills, lines 64–71][mapping-fill];
[annotation interpretation, lines 83–89][mapping-decisions];
[keyed deletions and renames, lines 143–163][mapping-apply];
[missing-code additions, lines 175–196][mapping-additions];
[individual corrections, lines 201–231][mapping-manual].

**Handoff:** `data/intermediate/mapping_gesis_dhis2_clean.csv`. Script 2 uses
it to assign clinic identities, and script 5 uses its 2018 records to recover
historical sectorization links. The new notebook exposes
`pipeline_xwalk_mapping_clean_df` for downstream targets.
See [legacy mapping output, lines 277–278][mapping-output];
[script 2 mapping use, lines 57–79][identity-mapping-input];
[script 5 historical mapping use, lines 309–328][sheds-mapping-input].

**Context for notebook 19:** each correction needs its source evidence, join
keys, expected effect, and a diagnostic. A GESIS code may legitimately map to
different UIDs over time, and a UID-year may retain multiple GESIS codes; a
global one-to-one assertion would change the legacy interpretation. The
notebook already separates the eight legacy stages and retains multiplicity
and name checks. Those checks document exceptions to interpret, not a reason
to merge or discard records automatically.
See [legacy multiplicity and name diagnostics, lines 235–274][mapping-diagnostics].

## 2 — Construct longitudinal clinic identities for Waves 1–2

**Source:** [2_wave1-2_construct_clinicID.R][legacy-identity].
**Destination:** [20_page-construct-clinic-ids.qmd](../20_page-construct-clinic-ids.qmd).

The script starts from an inventory of distinct clinic records in each monthly
file. The six identifying fields are clinic name, year, month, commune code,
facility code, and source-file number (`fname`). Its active code reads an
already saved inventory; the code that originally built that inventory is
commented out.
See [commented inventory construction and active read, lines 22–37][identity-inventory].

It corrects facility codes using the reviewed workbook and joins the cleaned
mapping by corrected code and mapping year. In 2015, January–March use old
GESIS codes and later months use new codes, except that records from `fname ==
1` retain the old codes. Three explicit exceptions prevent known incorrect
UID assignments. Within a corrected-code/name pair, it fills an unambiguous
UID, then fills missing type and mapped name from the group's mode. The mode
helper resolves ties by first occurrence, so input order matters.
See [code corrections, lines 42–50][identity-codes];
[2015 mapping and three exceptions, lines 63–79][identity-year-join];
[UID and attribute propagation, lines 98–125][identity-fill];
[mode tie behavior, lines 7–15][identity-mode].

The initial `clinic_ID` is the UID when available, otherwise corrected GESIS
code plus cleaned clinic name. The script marks reviewed deletions with a
missing ID, reconciles identities using verified shortened GESIS codes
("snips"), and then uses commune/name groups to reconcile remaining identities.
Four ambiguous snips and the 2014 `110543027` exception remain excluded from
the relevant reconciliation rules.
See [provisional identity, lines 143–156][identity-initial];
[reviewed deletions, lines 158–169][identity-deletions];
[verified snips and exclusions, lines 177–205][identity-snips];
[commune/name reconciliation and exception, lines 209–221][identity-commune].

**Handoff:** `data/intermediate/w2010_2019_clinicID.rds` and `.csv`, retaining
original matching fields, corrected code, mapped type, and `ID_checked`. That
flag records whether any mapped type in the identity group contains `CSB`;
it is not a general certification that the identity is correct. Scripts 4A,
6, and 7 consume this crosswalk.
See [ID_checked definition and crosswalk outputs, lines 223–233][identity-output].

**Context for notebook 20:** distinguish source inventory, code correction,
year-aware UID assignment, UID propagation, provisional identity, reviewed
deletion, and the two reconciliation steps. The current notebook rebuilds the
inventory from the staged ZIP in DuckDB, decoding Windows-1252 before reduction
and preserving file/row order. It contains both the newer Parquet correction
and mapping targets and the longer R transformation that repeats those
operations from the inventory. This duplication is an open refactoring
boundary: document which intermediate each later step should consume before
removing either route. Compare identities and exception records with the
legacy result, including missing IDs and mode ties.

## 3 — Construct the diagnosis dictionary across waves

**Source:** [3_construct_dictionary.R][legacy-dictionary].
**Proposed destination:** `21_page-construct-diagnosis-dictionary.qmd`.

This script defines comparable variables across Wave 1, Wave 2, Wave 3A
(2020), and Wave 3B (2021–2022). It combines the earlier-wave dictionary,
reviewed cross-wave diagnosis mappings, actual Wave 3 column names, a separate
2020 anemia export, and supplementary diagnoses. It replaces the original
Wave 1 diarrhea/pneumonia definitions and adds AVC and ULGEN entries that were
absent from the main dictionary.
See [source dictionaries and replacement diagnoses, lines 31–66][dictionary-inputs];
[AVC, ULGEN, and diarrhea/pneumonia additions, lines 69–92][dictionary-supplements].

It interprets mapping notation such as alternatives, ranges, and sums; joins
source descriptions to column identifiers; and aggregates source variables
into common definitions. The within-Wave-3 mapping handles changed age bands
and disease definitions, including anemia, severe acute malnutrition, and
suspected versus confirmed diabetes. It retains earlier-wave variables without
a Wave 3 match, excludes designated ignored categories, and assigns output
variable names such as `V1`, `V2`, and so on. These `V` variables identify
harmonized measurements; they have a different role from the Wave 3 source
table's `V1` row index.
See [within-Wave-3 definition changes, lines 105–162][dictionary-w3-map];
[common-definition aggregation, lines 178–205][dictionary-aggregate];
[mapping notation and wave joins, lines 208–277][dictionary-expressions];
[unmatched variables and V identifiers, lines 280–299][dictionary-variables].

The later stages enrich the dictionary with French and English descriptions,
diagnostic-code descriptions, reporting-table descriptions, available waves,
and output-file groups. They use existing translated material, live
`gtranslate` calls, and manual wording corrections. The `filename` column
partitions variables into 40 groups for diagnosis output.
See [existing translations and live diagnostic-code translations, lines 307–357][dictionary-translations];
[description assembly, wave availability, and output groups, lines 446–486][dictionary-enrichment];
[reporting-table translations and final wording corrections, lines 514–561][dictionary-tables].

**Handoff:** the active final write is `scratch/dictionary_test2.csv`, while
script 4A expects `data/clean/diagnosis_dictionary_translated.csv`. The missing
promotion or rename step is not established by this script. The dictionary's
per-wave expressions and `filename` assignments drive measurement cleaning.
See [dictionary scratch output, lines 580–581][dictionary-output];
[script 4A dictionary input, lines 29–31][diagnosis-dictionary-input].

**Context for the replacement:** explain source dictionaries and supplements,
cross-wave equivalence rules, expression construction, and descriptive
enrichment as separate stages. Wave 3 `X1`, `X2`, etc. are assigned from the
prepared table's column order, even though several joins now match on
descriptions. Record that schema explicitly so a changed reader or column
order cannot silently change a diagnosis. Preserve translation provenance
rather than treating a fresh network translation as a fixed input. Checks
should establish that referenced columns exist, summed terms are distinct,
and each source-expression mapping is used as intended.
See [positional X identifiers, lines 31–48][dictionary-w3-input];
[mapping uniqueness and repeated-summand checks, lines 563–578][dictionary-diagnostics].

## 4A — Clean measurements and combine reporting waves

**Source:** [4A_clean_clinic_diagnosis.R][legacy-diagnosis].
**Proposed destination:** `22_page-clean-clinic-diagnosis.qmd`.

This is the main measurement transformation. It consumes the clinic-ID
crosswalk, diagnosis dictionary, monthly tall Waves 1–2 files, prepared Wave 3
data, and supplementary AVC, diarrhea/pneumonia, and anemia exports. The
identity work determines which clinic a report belongs to; the dictionary
determines how its measurements become comparable variables.
See [identity and dictionary dependencies, lines 29–51][diagnosis-references];
[earlier-wave source files and supplements, lines 108–128][diagnosis-supplements].

For Waves 1–2, it replaces the superseded Wave 1 diarrhea/pneumonia records,
adds supplements, normalizes variable names, joins clinic IDs, and excludes
the explicitly problematic UID `qCHtCHkwqtQ`. It drops clinic-month/file groups
whose total reported value is not positive. Duplicate handling distinguishes
identical repeats, differences caused only by missing values, and distinct
values that the legacy rules sum. Unhandled conflicts receive the `-99`
sentinel. It then pivots measurements wide, adds expected but absent columns,
and evaluates the dictionary separately for the two waves.
See [supplements, identity join, exclusions, and reporting filter, lines 121–154][diagnosis-identity];
[duplicate classification and reductions, lines 160–196][diagnosis-duplicates];
[wide conversion and dictionary evaluation, lines 198–236][diagnosis-pivot].

For Wave 3, it inserts the separate 2020 anemia data, assigns the positional
`X` names expected by the dictionary, drops exact duplicate records, converts
negative values in three designated variables to missing, and removes rows
without positive measurements while excluding refrigerator-temperature fields
from that reporting check. It applies Wave 3A expressions to 2020 and Wave 3B
expressions to the later periods.
See [2020 anemia insertion, lines 271–287][diagnosis-anemia];
[column numbering, deduplication, negatives, and reporting filter, lines 293–324][diagnosis-w3-clean];
[Wave 3A and 3B evaluation, lines 329–344][diagnosis-w3-map].

Finally, it combines the waves and resolves overlapping reports using the
expected source file for each period. It prefers that file when present;
otherwise it keeps the closest available file number. The same selection
logic supplies the reporting-history table.
See [reporting-history selection, lines 350–373][diagnosis-tracker];
[combined outputs and overlapping-file selection, lines 382–418][diagnosis-combine].

**Handoff:** `data/clean/by_diagnosis/<filename>.feather`, separate
`<filename>_wrong_fname.feather` files for discarded overlapping reports, and
`data/clean/by_diagnosis/clinic_reporting_track.feather`. The tracking table
records which file supplied each clinic-month, using zero for no retained
report. Script 7 expects the tracker at
`data/intermediate/clinic_reporting_track.feather`; the source scripts do not
establish the intervening move or copy.
See [script 4A output directory, lines 22–25][diagnosis-output-dir];
[tracker values and write, lines 350–373][diagnosis-tracker];
[retained and rejected diagnosis outputs, lines 404–418][diagnosis-partitions];
[script 7 tracker input, line 21][metadata-tracker-input].

**Context for the replacement:** document earlier-wave cleaning, Wave 3
cleaning, dictionary application, report selection, and output partitioning
separately. The duplicate rules here differ from the maximum rule in script 0.
Missing values, entered zeros, the temporary `-1` missing-value sentinel, and
the `-99` conflict sentinel have different meanings. In sums, earlier-wave
`-1` values and Wave 3 missing values are replaced with zero; this does not
justify replacing every missing measurement with zero. Preserve the excluded
UID, negative-value rules, and `fname` tie behavior as explicit decisions to
review during migration.
See [wave-specific missing values in sums, lines 53–72][diagnosis-sum-missing];
[temporary -1 sentinel, lines 198–200][diagnosis-pivot-missing].

## 4B — Submit the diagnosis job to Slurm

**Source:** [4B_clean_clinic_diagnosis.slurm][legacy-slurm].
**Destination:** [Execute the Pipeline](../../releases/20_page-execute-pipeline.qmd)
and the [runtime runner](../../infrastructure/15_page-runner.qmd).

The launcher requests one node, four tasks, eight hours, and 48,000 MB on the
shared partition. It loads R 4.3, adjusts the user's R library path, and runs
script 4A with `R CMD BATCH`. It also configures job logs and email
notifications. It contributes execution settings rather than an additional
scientific transformation.
See [resources, logs, and notification settings, lines 2–10][slurm-allocation];
[R environment and batch command, lines 12–17][slurm-execution].

**Handoff:** execution of script 4A and its log files. The scientific artifacts
are produced by 4A, not by a separate cleaning operation in this launcher.

**Context for the replacement:** the execution page owns how the targets graph
is launched, while the runner supplies the project runtime. Record the Slurm
allocation and target-worker settings when diagnosis work is added; four
requested tasks do not alone configure a parallel targets backend. The
legacy launcher's allocation and 4A's `future` worker configuration must be
considered together when reproducing its execution.
See [script 4A worker and globals settings, lines 18–20][diagnosis-workers].

## 5 — Reconcile sectorization and construct 2022 healthsheds

**Source:** [5_clean_sect2022_construct_healthsheds.R][legacy-sheds].
**Proposed destination:** `23_page-construct-healthsheds.qmd`.

This script connects the 2022 sectorization's FKT assignments to administrative
polygons, then unions the assigned polygons for each clinic. Its inputs include
the sectorization table, OCHA/BNGRC boundaries and code lookup, reviewed matching
files, manual geolocation corrections, the 2018 sectorization, and the cleaned
GESIS–DHIS2 mapping.
See [spatial sources and sectorization schema, lines 54–100][sheds-inputs];
[2018 sectorization and cleaned facility mapping, lines 309–328][sheds-mapping-input].

It first repairs geometry and separates Nosy Mitsio from a mainland polygon.
It reconciles duplicated FKT codes while preserving the reviewed population
totals, validates original codes, and fills missing matches from several
rounds of reviewed fuzzy and manual matching. It attaches polygons and uses
their topological relationships to identify isolated assignments. Some
isolated matches are removed while explicitly protected manual matches remain.
See [geometry repair and Nosy Mitsio split, lines 56–88][sheds-geometry];
[duplicate FKT and population rules, lines 102–121][sheds-duplicates];
[reviewed matching rounds and geometry joins, lines 123–228][sheds-matching];
[topology checks and isolated-match removal, lines 230–275][sheds-isolated].

Later passes recover assignments using the 2018 sectorization, apply further
manual matches and unmatches, and assign some remaining polygons through a
close commune-name match when that commune has one clinic and the assignment
does not worsen contiguity. Subsequent reviewed corrections move FKT between
clinics, resolve duplicates, and split coastal islands into separately
assigned geometry. The script records matching provenance in `match_type` and
rebuilds healthsheds after successive correction passes.
See [2018 recovery, lines 304–404][sheds-historical];
[manual matches and unmatches, lines 406–459][sheds-manual];
[commune matches and contiguity guard, lines 481–565][sheds-commune];
[reviewed reassignments and duplicates, lines 585–664][sheds-reviewed];
[coastal-island splits, lines 666–720][sheds-islands];
[final reassignments and aggregation, lines 722–786][sheds-final-fixes].

The `sect_to_shed()` helper unions assigned polygons by facility UID,
calculates population from distinct FKT UID/population pairs, and records
matched-area counts, connected components, and polygon parts. Reviewed shared
assignments can produce overlapping healthsheds; this is not simply a
non-overlapping partition of Madagascar.
See [population, geometry, components, and polygon parts, lines 10–44][sheds-aggregation];
[reviewed shared assignments, lines 102–105][sheds-overlaps].

**Handoff:** `data/intermediate/sectorization2022_cleaned.feather`,
`data/intermediate/sectorization2022_cleaned_shapefile`, and
`data/clean/healthsheds2022` plus `healthsheds2022.rds`. It also writes review
maps and unmatched-clinic tables under `scratch/`. Scripts 6 and 7 consume
the cleaned sectorization and healthsheds.
See [review maps and unmatched-clinic export, lines 805–967][sheds-review-outputs];
[sectorization and healthshed outputs, lines 969–1000][sheds-outputs].

**Context for the replacement:** organize the narrative around source geometry,
matching evidence, assignment corrections, catchment aggregation, and residual
exceptions. Preserve the precedence of correction rounds, population counting,
overlap policy, island splits, and the distinction between connected components
and polygon parts. The legacy comments report residual non-contiguous
healthsheds even after all polygons are assigned; complete coverage and
contiguity are separate properties. A shapefile is a group of companion files,
so artifact tracking must cover the complete dataset.
See [historical residual-contiguity and coverage observations, lines 788–803][sheds-residuals].

## 6 — Compare location sources and select clinic coordinates

**Source:** [6_locate_clinics.R][legacy-location].
**Proposed destination:** `24_page-locate-clinics.qmd`.

This script assembles candidate coordinates from the cleaned sectorization,
MDDSS, WHO and UNICEF master lists, and a separate GPS source, using the
clinic-ID crosswalk to connect historical GESIS codes to UIDs. It cleans
coordinate formats, applies specific UID and duplicate-record corrections,
and uses closest-name matches where a GESIS code has multiple possible
identity matches. It also identifies likely clinic FKT by name and reported
distance within the sectorization.
See [source reads and sectorization coordinates, lines 50–103][location-inputs];
[MDDSS identity and closest-name joins, lines 105–136][location-mdss];
[WHO corrections and coordinates, lines 138–180][location-who];
[UNICEF and GPS candidates, lines 182–211][location-unicef-gps];
[FKT name/distance selection, lines 228–256][location-fkt].

It converts candidates to spatial points and tests whether each lies inside
the matched FKT or the clinic's healthshed. The selection rule first prefers
WHO, sectorization, UNICEF, then MDDSS points contained in the matched FKT;
it also considers GPS points contained in the healthshed. It then considers
other points contained in the healthshed in the listed source order. If no
point qualifies, it falls back to the matched FKT centroid, then the
healthshed centroid, and finally an explicit missing-location state.
See [point conversion, containment, and source comparison, lines 273–312][location-containment];
[coordinate-source precedence and centroid fallbacks, lines 314–329][location-selection].

**Handoff:** `data/intermediate/clinic_LL.rds`, retaining candidate coordinates,
containment evidence, FKT geometry, and the selected-source label `which_use`.
Labels ending in `2` indicate selection through the later healthshed-based
test. Script 7 uses these labels to extract the final coordinates.
See [selected-source labels, lines 314–329][location-selection];
[location artifact write, lines 331–334][location-output].

**Context for the replacement:** explain candidate ingestion, identity matching,
spatial comparison, and selection separately. The introductory source list is
not the final selection policy; the actual `which_use` conditions are the
operative rule. Name similarity helps join candidate records but does not
independently establish that a coordinate is correct. Keep source provenance
and distinguish a reported facility point from an inferred centroid. Document
the coordinate reference system and preserve explicit unresolved cases.

## 7 — Combine reporting and spatial clinic metadata

**Source:** [7_combine_clinic_metadata.R][legacy-metadata].
**Proposed destination:** `25_page-combine-clinic-metadata.qmd`.

This script brings the measurement and spatial branches together. It reads
the reporting tracker from 4A, clinic identities from 2, sectorization and
healthsheds from 5, and candidate/selected coordinates from 6. Its two products
have different row definitions.
See [metadata dependencies, lines 21–29][metadata-inputs].

The reporting metadata has one clinic-year-month record derived from the
tracker. It adds the original GESIS database code for earlier records and
uses the clinic UID for reported months from 2020 onward when that code is
otherwise missing. `fname` remains available to show reporting source and
absence of a retained report.
See [monthly reporting and database-code rules, lines 37–53][metadata-temporal].

The spatial metadata summarizes reporting duration, first and last reporting
month, and number of reporting months by clinic. It prefers 2022 sectorization
for clinic name, type, status, and administrative attributes, then falls back
to the latest historical clinic-ID record. It adds healthshed geometry,
extracts coordinates from the chosen source or a centroid, applies the
legacy public/private fallback rules, and joins reviewed neighbor-clinic
pairings for facilities without their own healthshed. It records whether a
healthshed exists and which GPS source was used.
See [reporting summary and attribute precedence, lines 67–93][metadata-summary];
[geometry join and coordinate extraction, lines 95–122][metadata-coordinates];
[ownership fallback, neighbor pairing, and provenance, lines 124–138][metadata-fallbacks].

**Handoff:** `data/clean/clinic_reporting_metadata.csv` and
`data/clean/clinic_spatial_metadata.csv`. Geometry is dropped before writing
the spatial CSV; the healthshed geometry remains a separate spatial product.
See [metadata exports and geometry removal, lines 148–154][metadata-output].

**Context for the replacement:** define temporal and clinic-level outputs
separately and document source precedence for each field. Public/private
fallbacks based on `ID_checked` and absence from 2022 sectorization are legacy
heuristics, not observations of ownership in every year. Check that every
location label emitted by script 6 has a corresponding extraction rule here:
the legacy script 6 can select UNICEF, but script 7's coordinate cases do not
include UNICEF. Document that discrepancy before choosing whether parity or
a corrected result is the migration criterion.
See [script 6 UNICEF selection, lines 314–329][location-selection];
[script 7 coordinate cases without UNICEF, lines 98–112][metadata-coordinate-cases].

## Shared utilities — Make helper semantics visible where used

**Source:** [999_utility_functions.R][legacy-utilities].
**Destinations:** [18_page-prep-w3.qmd](../18_page-prep-w3.qmd) and proposed
`23_page-construct-healthsheds.qmd`, according to the helper's role.

The utility file defines a Malagasy-to-French cardinal-direction lookup,
`grouped_stringdist_fulljoin()`, and `read_csv_nonlogical()`. The grouped join
nests records within administrative groups, generates fuzzy string matches,
allows a caller-supplied rule to select candidates, and optionally unnests
the result. Its method and thresholds affect which spatial matches are
considered. The CSV reader changes inferred logical columns to numeric to
protect sparse measurement columns.
See [direction lookup, lines 1–9][utilities-directions];
[grouped fuzzy join and parameters, lines 12–44][utilities-matching];
[sparse-column reader, lines 47–62][utilities-reader].

**Handoff:** functions and a lookup table sourced into an R session rather
than a persisted data product. Script 5 calls the grouped matching helper.
Other scripts duplicate the CSV reader, and scripts 2 and 6 define their own
mode helpers outside this utility file.
See [script 5 grouped matching call, lines 356–367][sheds-helper-call];
[script 2 mode helper, lines 7–15][identity-mode];
[script 6 mode helper, lines 12–20][location-mode].

**Context for the replacements:** document helper behavior next to its first
scientific use, including grouping keys, thresholds, missing-value behavior,
and tie rules. The CSV-reader responsibility already has a DuckDB adaptation
in notebook 18. Script 5 sources `scripts/0_utility_functions.R`, but the
archived file here is named `999_utility_functions.R`; record the actual
dependency when migrating rather than reproducing an unresolved source path.
A shared code module can be extracted later if repeated use warrants it.
See [mismatched legacy utility source path, line 54][sheds-helper-source].

## Exploratory checks — Recover questions and reproducible comparisons

**Source:** [data_checks.R][legacy-checks].
**Destinations:** [17_page-inspect-source-data.qmd](../17_page-inspect-source-data.qmd),
checks in the notebooks owning each transformation, and proposed
`26_page-validate-migration.qmd`.

This is a collection of investigations rather than one ordered production
stage. It compares files and column names between 2021–2022 exports, 2023
exports, and a later 2023 delivery; compares clinic/period coverage and values;
and explores CSV type inference under different readers and sampling limits.
Later sections compare old and rebuilt Wave 3 tables and ordered versus
unordered diagnosis dictionaries, tracing differences in missing values,
column types, names, and individual measurements back to source exports.
Several investigations are repeated with different local file paths.
See [export and column inventories, lines 10–116][checks-schema];
[coverage and value comparisons, lines 119–266][checks-coverage];
[reader and type-inference experiments, lines 268–338][checks-types];
[Wave 3 comparisons and source tracing, lines 357–613][checks-w3];
[dictionary comparisons and repeated investigations, lines 653–902][checks-dictionaries].

The final section also performs a data transformation: it splits a combined
2021–2022 mumps export into separate year files and writes a 2021 subset
containing the male 2–11-month variable plus metadata. Those writes go into
the legacy raw directory. They should be accounted for as derived artifacts
with a source dependency in the replacement workflow, rather than remaining
an undocumented prerequisite.
See [mumps source, year split, and exports, lines 912–935][checks-mumps-split];
[male 2–11-month subset and export, lines 938–954][checks-mumps-subset].

**Handoff:** mostly printed comparisons and interactive inspection, plus the
three mumps CSV outputs. There is no single reusable validation report or
uniform pass/fail contract in this file.

**Context for the replacements:** put source schema and coverage questions in
notebook 17, preserve focused invariants with the transformation they test,
and use the proposed validation notebook to record comparisons between
equivalent legacy and replacement artifacts. Identify the exact source
versions, align records by scientific keys, and compare missingness as well
as values. Account for legitimate schema/format changes separately from
scientific differences. Turning every exploratory statement into an
automated assertion would preserve unfinished investigations as assumptions.

## Assignment-to-target inventory

This inventory maps the legacy assignments to named responsibilities in the
replacement graph. It is a design index; no targets are created or rewired
by these tables.

Identifiers use `script::variable`, for example `1::mapping`. The script keys
match the filenames in the crosswalk; `999` denotes the utilities and `checks`
denotes `data_checks.R`. A repeated variable is qualified by its stage because
an in-place reassignment can represent a different scientific operation.
Function-local values are listed with their owning operation, and short
setup/read/normalization steps may share one target. Columns created inside
`mutate()`, `summarise()`, or `:=` belong to the assigned table; the important
column stages are named in the rows rather than proposed as individual targets.
Commented-out alternatives are not active assignments; the commented inventory
builder in script 2 is retained as provenance for its active inventory read.

**Existing** means the exact name is declared in the current pipeline notebooks
or `_targets.R`; it does not establish that the target has completed. A row
can map to an existing target that already groups several legacy operations.
Where the new pipeline changes storage or avoids a large intermediate, the
mapping identifies the owning transformation, not an identical R object.
**Recommended** names describe results or responsibilities still to be
introduced or separated from a coarse target. Names shared across scripts
identify the same producer/consumer handoff, not duplicate proposed targets.
Recommended names leave storage format and branching undecided.

Helper definitions are dependencies of their owning data targets, not proposed
targets that simply cache functions. Diagnostic and exploratory objects are
identified explicitly. Their inclusion preserves the question being asked;
it does not promote every scratch expression to a validated scientific rule.
The input inventories and current file selectors remain the common staging
boundary. Rows for final writes are included even when the legacy write call
has no assigned return value, so the data handoff has a target name too.

### Script 4B — Slurm launcher

This file contains no R variable assignments. Its shell assignment to
`R_LIBS_USER` and its resource directives belong to the existing runtime and
execution notebooks, rather than to a scientific data target. The job executes
the responsibilities mapped under script 4A, including recommended
`pipeline_diagnosis_output_paths` and `pipeline_clinic_reporting_track_path`.
See [the launcher][legacy-slurm].

| `checks::equals_na`; `checks::mismatches`; `checks::out`; `checks::all_mismatches`; `checks::rownames(all_mismatches) (second block)` | Repeated NA-aware mismatch construction; keep separate ownership from the measurement-table comparison. | `pipeline_dictionary_legacy_value_mismatches` | Recommended | [815–854][assign-checks-815-854], [856][assign-checks-856-856] |
| `checks::test1`; `checks::test2 (repeated source readers and schema)` | Repeated explicit-numeric/base/schema reads grouped with the CSV-reader investigation. | `pipeline_csv_reader_comparison` | Recommended | [864–868][assign-checks-864-868], [878–889][assign-checks-878-889] |
| `checks::input_path`; `checks::file1` | Identify and read the combined-year mumps supplement. | `pipeline_mumps_source` | Recommended | [912–915][assign-checks-912-915] |
| `checks::file_2021`; `checks::file_2022` | Split the mumps supplement by reporting year; both short filters share one target. | `pipeline_mumps_by_year` | Recommended | [918–919][assign-checks-918-919] |
| `checks::target_col`; `checks::metadata_cols`; `checks::file_2021_males_2_11m` | Select the 2021 male 2–11-month variable with its source metadata. | `pipeline_mumps_2021_males_2_11m` | Recommended | [939–943][assign-checks-939-943] |
| `checks::file_2021 -> CSV`; `checks::file_2022 -> CSV`; `checks::file_2021_males_2_11m -> CSV` | Group the three related derived-output paths. | `pipeline_mumps_output_paths` | Recommended | [922–935][assign-checks-922-935], [948–954][assign-checks-948-954] |

For notebook 20, the recommended UID-fill and provisional-ID stages sit
between the existing mapped-clinic-month output and the existing coarse
`pipeline_clinic_ids_corrected_df` output. The recommended snip stage would
similarly expose part of `pipeline_clinic_ids_reconciled_df`. The table records
these boundaries without choosing which current route to replace.

## Handoffs to resolve as the notebooks develop

These observations explain where a literal script-for-script translation
would leave important behavior implicit. They are review items, not changes
implemented by this page.

| Handoff or decision | Evidence in the current source | What the owning notebook needs to record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prepared Wave 3 artifact | Script 0 writes a dated filename; scripts 3 and 4A read the generic `wave3_with_keys.csv` ([0:274–275][w3-output]; [3:31–48][dictionary-w3-input]; [4A:249–249][diagnosis-w3-input]) | Which prepared artifact and source schema supply both dictionary construction and measurement cleaning |
| Reporting tracker artifact | Script 4A writes under `data/clean/by_diagnosis/`; script 7 reads under `data/intermediate/` ([4A:22–25][diagnosis-output-dir]; [4A:350–373][diagnosis-tracker]; [7:21][metadata-tracker-input]) | The authoritative reporting-tracker artifact and its dependency in metadata assembly |
| Diagnosis dictionary artifact | Script 3 writes `scratch/dictionary_test2.csv`; 4A reads `data/clean/diagnosis_dictionary_translated.csv` ([3:580–581][dictionary-output]; [4A:29–31][diagnosis-dictionary-input]) | Which reviewed dictionary is authoritative and how it becomes an input to cleaning |
| Raw versus cleaned facility mapping | Script 0 reads the original mapping; scripts 2 and 5 read the cleaned mapping ([0:191–212][w3-crosswalk]; [2:57–79][identity-mapping-input]; [5:309–328][sheds-mapping-input]) | Why each join uses that version, its year rules, and its expected cardinality |
| Clinic-ID transformation route | Notebook 20 contains both Parquet stages and an R stage repeating the corrections and mapping join | The intended input and output of each stage, before consolidating duplicate work |
| Positional diagnosis names | Script 3 assigns `X` names from Wave 3 column order; 4A independently recreates them ([3:31–48][dictionary-w3-input]; [4A:293–324][diagnosis-w3-clean]) | A shared, recorded column-name mapping that permits comparison after storage changes |
| Missing values and duplicates | Script 0 takes maxima; 4A uses conditional deduplication, summation, and sentinels ([0:161–168][w3-max]; [4A:160–196][diagnosis-duplicates]; [4A:53–72][diagnosis-sum-missing]) | Which rule applies at each row definition, and why |
| Spatial source dependency | Script 5 sources `0_utility_functions.R`; the available utility file is `999_utility_functions.R` ([5:54–54][sheds-helper-source]; [999:1–62][legacy-utilities]) | The actual helper implementation and matching parameters |
| Coordinate extraction | Script 6 can select UNICEF; script 7 has no corresponding coordinate case ([6:314–329][location-selection]; [7:98–112][metadata-coordinate-cases]) | Whether to preserve the legacy missing result or adopt an explicitly reviewed correction |
| Mumps supplements | `data_checks.R` writes derived year/subset files back into the raw tree ([data_checks:912–935][checks-mumps-split]; [data_checks:938–954][checks-mumps-subset]) | The source export, transformation, and derived-output destination |
| Output validation | Legacy scripts mix diagnostic queries, comments, and scratch exports ([1:235–274][mapping-diagnostics]; [3:563–578][dictionary-diagnostics]; [data_checks:357–613][checks-w3]) | Which evidence establishes equivalence, which differences are intentional, and which remain unresolved |

The summaries and source links preserve the context needed to work through
these decisions notebook by notebook. Revisit the migration-state column when
a destination is created or its equivalence evidence is recorded.
